title: Plant Water Balance
subtitle: Transpiration, cohesion-tension, stomata and Australian plant adaptations
subject: Biology
syllabusModule: Module 8 Non-infectious Disease and Disorders (2017) + Cells to systems and Evolution and ecosystems (2025)
syllabusDotPoints: mechanisms in plants that allow water balance to be maintained (ACSBL115)
Use the cohesion-tension theory to explain how osmotic pressure, transpiration stream and the cohesion of water molecules control the movement of water and dissolved minerals through the xylem
Explain how light, temperature, wind and humidity affect the rate of transpiration in plants
Conduct a practical investigation to demonstrate the effect of an environmental factor on the rate of transpiration
Conduct a practical investigation to examine structural adaptations for water balance in Australian plants
inquiryQuestion: How is an organism's internal environment maintained in response to a changing external environment?
lessonIntent: Students can explain water movement with the cohesion-tension theory, explain how light, temperature, wind and humidity affect transpiration, describe stomatal control, and link Australian plant structures to reduced water loss.
examSkill: Explain a transpiration factor or a water-saving adaptation by its mechanism, always linking it to the water vapour gradient, stomata or surface area, and calculate a transpiration rate from potometer data.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, transpiration and plant water balance. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: A hundred metres, no pump
scenes.body: Centurion, a mountain ash in Tasmania, stands close to 100 metres tall. Every leaf at the top still gets water from the soil.
scenes.callout: How does water climb a tree with no heart and no pump?
scenes.caption: Tall trees such as Tasmania's mountain ash lift water about 100 metres without a pump.

voiceover.text: In southern Tasmania there's a mountain ash called Centurion, and it stands close to one hundred metres tall, one of the tallest flowering plants on Earth. Every leaf at the very top still needs water from the soil, and the tree lifts it all that way without a heart, without muscles and without any pump. At the same time, plants in dry parts of Australia have to hang on to every drop they have. So today we'll answer two questions. How does water actually move up a plant, and how do plants, especially Australian ones, control how much of it they lose?

scenes.heading: The cohesion-tension theory
scenes.body: Evaporation from the leaves pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem.

bullets.text: Roots take up mineral ions, so water enters root cells by osmosis.
Water evaporates from leaf cells and diffuses out through the stomata: transpiration.
This creates tension that pulls water up the xylem, carrying dissolved minerals.
Cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) keeps the column unbroken.

scenes.callout: Water is pulled from the top, not pushed from the bottom.
scenes.caption: Transpiration pulls a cohesive column of water and minerals up the xylem from the roots.

voiceover.text: OK, so how does water climb a tree? The accepted explanation is the cohesion tension theory, and it works from the top down. Inside the leaf, water evaporates from the moist cell walls and diffuses out through the stomata. That loss of water vapour is called transpiration. As water leaves, it pulls on the water behind it, creating a tension, a kind of suction, in the xylem vessels. That pull can travel all the way down because of cohesion. Water molecules are held to each other by hydrogen bonds, so the column in the xylem doesn't break, and they also cling to the xylem walls. At the bottom, the roots take up mineral ions, which makes water enter the root cells by osmosis. The result is a continuous transpiration stream from soil to leaf, carrying dissolved minerals up with the water.

scenes.heading: What speeds up transpiration?
scenes.body: Transpiration depends on how open the stomata are and how steep the water vapour gradient is.

bullets.text: Light: stomata open in light, so transpiration increases.
Temperature: warmer water evaporates and diffuses faster.
Wind: carries humid air away from the leaf, steepening the gradient.
Humidity: moist air makes the gradient shallower, so transpiration slows.

scenes.callout: Three factors speed it up. High humidity slows it down.
scenes.caption: Light, heat and wind increase transpiration; high humidity decreases it.

voiceover.text: Now, the rate of transpiration isn't fixed. It depends on two things, how open the stomata are, and how steep the gradient of water vapour is between the inside of the leaf and the air outside. Light increases the rate, because stomata open in the light to let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis. A higher temperature increases it too, because water evaporates and diffuses faster, and warm air can hold more water vapour. Wind increases the rate by blowing away the layer of humid air that builds up around the leaf, which keeps the gradient steep. Humidity works the other way. When the air is already moist, the gradient is shallow, so transpiration slows down. So in an exam answer, always link the factor to either the stomata or the gradient.

scenes.heading: Stomata: the plant's control valves
scenes.body: Guard cells open and close the leaf pores by pumping potassium ions, which moves water and changes their turgor.

bullets.text: To open: guard cells take up potassium ions, water follows by osmosis, turgor rises and the pore opens.
To close in drought: the hormone ABA makes potassium ions leave, water follows, and the pore shuts.
Water always moves by osmosis; the plant controls it by moving ions.

scenes.secondary: Closing stomata saves water but also blocks carbon dioxide entry for photosynthesis, the central trade-off plants must manage.
scenes.callout: Move the ions, water follows, the pore opens or shuts.
scenes.caption: Guard cells move potassium ions; water follows by osmosis to open or close the stoma.

voiceover.text: So how does a plant control its water loss from moment to moment? Through the stomata, controlled by a pair of guard cells around each pore. To open a stoma, the guard cells take up potassium ions, using energy from A T P. Water follows those ions in by osmosis, the guard cells swell with higher turgor, and they bow apart to open the pore. When the plant is short of water, it makes a hormone called A B A, which causes potassium ions to leave the guard cells. Water follows them out, the guard cells go limp, and the pore closes. Notice the plant never pumps water directly. It moves ions, and water follows by osmosis. And there's a trade off, because closing the stomata saves water but also shuts out the carbon dioxide the plant needs for photosynthesis.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Transpiration: loss of water vapour from the leaves, mainly through the stomata.
Transpiration stream: the continuous flow of water and minerals from roots to leaves in the xylem.
Cohesion: attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonding.
Guard cells: paired cells that change turgor to open or close a stoma.
Xerophyte: a plant structurally adapted to survive in dry environments.

scenes.callout: Transpiration is the loss. The transpiration stream is the flow it drives.
scenes.caption: Transpiration, transpiration stream, cohesion, guard cells and xerophyte.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the key terms. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves, mainly through the stomata. The transpiration stream is the continuous flow of water and dissolved minerals from the roots up to the leaves through the xylem, the flow that transpiration drives. Cohesion is the attraction between water molecules, caused by hydrogen bonding, and it's what keeps the water column in one piece. Guard cells are the paired cells that change their turgor to open or close a stoma. And a xerophyte is a plant that's structurally adapted to survive in dry environments, which is where we're heading next.

scenes.heading: Australian plants built for dry country
scenes.body: Many Australian plants have permanent structures that reduce water loss by cutting the gradient, the heat load or the surface area.

bullets.text: Eucalypts: leaves hang vertically and have a thick waxy cuticle, reducing midday heating and evaporation.
Banksias: stomata sunken in hairy pits that trap humid air, reducing the gradient.
Spinifex: leaves roll up, enclosing the stomata and cutting exposed surface area.

scenes.secondary: In the lab, examine leaf cross sections or epidermal peels under a microscope and link each structure to its effect on water loss.
scenes.callout: Name the feature, then the physical reason it cuts water loss.
scenes.caption: Eucalypts, banksias and spinifex show structural adaptations that reduce water loss.

voiceover.text: Now let's look at Australian plants, because the syllabus asks you to examine them. Many have permanent structures that cut water loss all the time, not just when stomata close. Adult eucalyptus leaves often hang vertically, edge on to the midday sun, so they absorb less heat, and a thick waxy cuticle stops water escaping through the leaf surface. Many banksias have their stomata sunken in pits lined with hairs. Those pits trap a pocket of humid air, so the water vapour gradient is smaller and less water leaves. And spinifex, the grass of the desert, rolls its leaves inwards, enclosing the stomata and cutting the surface exposed to dry air. In the lab you'd look at leaf sections under a microscope, and the exam technique is the same. Name the feature, then give the physical reason it reduces water loss.

scenes.heading: Measuring transpiration with a potometer
scenes.question: In a bubble potometer, the air bubble moved 24 mm in 10 minutes in still air, and 60 mm in 10 minutes with a fan blowing on the leaves. Calculate each rate and explain the difference.
scenes.coachNote: Rate = distance ÷ time. Then link wind to the water vapour gradient.
steps: Still air: rate = 24 mm ÷ 10 min = 2.4 mm/min.
With fan: rate = 60 mm ÷ 10 min = 6.0 mm/min.
The fan increased the rate 2.5 times (6.0 ÷ 2.4).
Wind removes the humid air around the leaf, steepening the water vapour gradient, so more water is lost and taken up.
Answer: 2.4 mm/min vs 6.0 mm/min; wind increases transpiration ✓
scenes.caption: Still air 2.4 mm/min, with fan 6.0 mm/min: wind increases transpiration.

voiceover.text: Let's work through a practical, because you may run this one yourself. A bubble potometer measures how fast a leafy shoot takes up water, which tracks transpiration closely, since most of the water taken up is lost from the leaves. In still air, the bubble moves twenty four millimetres in ten minutes. With a fan blowing on the leaves, it moves sixty millimetres in ten minutes. Rate is distance divided by time, so in still air that's two point four millimetres per minute, and with the fan it's six point zero millimetres per minute, two and a half times faster. Why? The wind removes the humid air around the leaf, keeping the water vapour gradient steep, so more water evaporates and more is drawn up. For a fair test, only the wind should change, with light, temperature and humidity kept the same.

scenes.heading: Three traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: writing that guard cells pump water to open stomata. They take up potassium ions, and water follows by osmosis.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: saying roots push water up the tree. The main force is the pull from transpiration at the leaves. Trap 3: saying humid air speeds up transpiration. High humidity makes the vapour gradient smaller, so transpiration slows.
scenes.callout: Ions move, water follows. Pulled from the top. Humidity slows it.
scenes.caption: Guard cells move ions, not water; water is pulled up by transpiration; humidity slows transpiration.

voiceover.text: Three traps. Trap one, writing that guard cells pump water to open the stomata. They don't. Guard cells take up potassium ions, and water follows by osmosis, so the ion movement is what the plant controls. Trap two, saying the roots push water up the tree. Roots do take in water by osmosis, but the main force lifting water up the xylem is the pull created by transpiration at the leaves, which is the whole point of the cohesion tension theory. Trap three, getting humidity backwards. Humid air doesn't speed transpiration up. It makes the water vapour gradient smaller, so transpiration slows down, which is why plants lose less water on a muggy day.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Two leaves are identical except one has sunken stomata. On a hot, dry, windy day, which loses water more slowly, and what is the mechanism?
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause and think about the diffusion gradient.
answerSteps: Transpiration depends on the water vapour gradient between the leaf interior and the air outside.
Sunken stomata sit in pits that trap a layer of humid air right at the pore.
That humid pocket reduces the steepness of the diffusion gradient for water vapour leaving.
Wind cannot strip that trapped humid air away as easily, so loss stays lower.
Answer: the sunken-stomata leaf loses water more slowly, by reducing the diffusion gradient ✓
scenes.caption: Sunken stomata trap humid air, reducing the water-vapour gradient.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Two leaves are identical except one has sunken stomata. On a hot, dry, windy day, which loses water more slowly, and what's the mechanism? Pause and think about the diffusion gradient. Right, let's check it. Transpiration depends on the gradient of water vapour between the moist inside of the leaf and the drier air outside, and the steeper the gradient, the faster water leaves. Sunken stomata sit at the bottom of little pits, and those pits trap a pocket of humid air right at the pore, which makes the gradient less steep. And because that air is tucked down in the pit, the wind can't strip it away as easily. So the leaf with sunken stomata loses water more slowly, because it reduces the water vapour gradient at the pore.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Cohesion-tension: transpiration pulls a cohesive column of water and minerals up the xylem.
Light, temperature and wind increase transpiration; high humidity decreases it.
Guard cells move potassium ions and water follows by osmosis; ABA closes stomata in drought.
Eucalypts, banksias and spinifex have structures that reduce heat load, the vapour gradient or surface area.
A potometer measures water uptake as a stand-in for the rate of transpiration.
scenes.finalPrompt: Explaining any water adaptation or factor? Name it, then link it to the stomata, the vapour gradient or the surface area.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: cohesion-tension, transpiration factors, stomata, Australian adaptations, the potometer.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five takeaways. First, the cohesion tension theory. Transpiration at the leaves pulls a cohesive column of water and minerals up the xylem. Second, light, temperature and wind all increase the rate of transpiration, while high humidity decreases it. Third, guard cells control the stomata by moving potassium ions, water follows by osmosis, and A B A closes them in a drought. Fourth, Australian plants like eucalypts, banksias and spinifex have structures that cut their heat load, the vapour gradient or their exposed surface area. And fifth, a potometer measures water uptake, which we use to estimate the rate of transpiration. Whenever you explain a factor or an adaptation, link it to the stomata, the gradient or the surface area.
